entry.title: dffy: a diff viewer for the terminal
entry.summary: dffy is a terminal diff viewer written in Rust. File tree, search, syntax-aware diffs and an engine that opens the Linux kernel's 13,168 changed files in under 10 ms. It has replaced delta as my git pager.
entry.content:
I've changed diff programs. I'd been using delta as my git pager for years, and for a loose diff it's perfect, but it isn't a viewer: it's a colouriser. When the change spans thirty files and I want to get to the one that matters, delta gives me no tree, no search, no way to jump between files. That's what I was missing.

That something is dffy, a terminal diff viewer written in Rust. I run it inside the repo and it opens the change full screen: file tree on the left, diff on the right, split or unified. Pipe something into it and it prints the diff like any pager.

What it is¶

A native binary, no runtime behind it, doing three things at once: interactive viewer, git pager and diff generator for scripts. It has its own diff engine (histogram plus a syntax one) and its own terminal renderer, with no TUI framework in between.

What made me switch:

  • Incremental start. It doesn't compute the whole diff before painting: it shows the first files as soon as it finds them and keeps working on the rest in the background. The Linux kernel's v6.0..v6.1 range is 13,168 files and a 48 MB patch, and the first changed line is on screen in under 10 ms. With --watch it repaints as you edit, stage and commit.
  • Real navigation. File tree, fuzzy picker on o, search across the whole diff with /, v in the tree to mark files as viewed. Each file opens at its first change, and n/N jump change to change, crossing into the next file when needed.
  • Syntax-aware diff. d swaps the engine: it emphasises only the tokens that actually change (even when they've been reordered), dims code that was only reformatted (~) and marks statements or items that moved with ». It's what difftastic does, but inside the same viewer.
  • Staged, unstaged and untracked in one view, each file tagged with its state. Plus conflicted files from a merge, rebase or cherry-pick, with the conflict markers highlighted.
  • Split or unified picked automatically from the terminal width, highlighting for 30 languages, and the changed word emphasised inside the line.

Install¶

On macOS, as a cask:

brew install --cask amalucelli/tap/dffy

On Linux I used the official script, which drops it in ~/.local/bin/dffy:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amalucelli/dffy/main/install.sh | sh

I'm on 0.2.1.

Usage¶

dffy                        # staged, unstaged and untracked
dffy --staged               # what's in the index
dffy HEAD~3                 # a revision against the working tree
dffy main...feature         # changes since the merge base
dffy show HEAD              # a commit with its message
dffy main.. -- src/         # limited to a path
dffy a.txt b.txt            # two files or folders, no repo needed
dffy --watch                # refresh on every change
dffy --syntax v6.0 v6.1     # diff by syntax, not by lines
dffy --stat main..          # also --name-only, --name-status, --exit-code

Inside the viewer almost everything is a single key: n/N between changes, f/F between files, / searches, o opens the picker, s cycles the layout, W wraps long lines, d turns on the syntax diff, space opens the command panel, ? lists the keys in effect and q quits.

As git's pager¶

This is the bit that replaces delta:

git config --global core.pager dffy
git config --global interactive.diffFilter "dffy --color-only"

The --color-only matters because it preserves the line count (38 in, 38 out), which is what git add -p needs to avoid complaining about "mismatched output". And as a difftool:

git config --global difftool.dffy.cmd 'dffy "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"'
git config --global difftool.prompt false
git difftool --tool=dffy -d main    # every file at once, as two folders

I also wired it into my ai-diff script, which now renders the preview with dffy --color=always --paging=never.

For scripts and agents¶

Two outputs that have nothing to do with the TUI:

dffy --json main.. | jq -c 'select(.type == "file") | {path, added, removed}'

--json emits JSON Lines: a header, one line per file with its hunks and, for every diff line, its kind (added, removed, context), whether it's paired with its edit and the column ranges that were touched. That's what I use when I want an agent to read a diff without swallowing 40 MB of text.

The other one is dffy mcp, a MCP server that lets an agent list a change's files and read its diffs a page at a time, instead of dumping the whole patch into the prompt.

Configuration¶

Everything lives in ~/.config/dffy/config, as key = value lines, so it can go in your dotfiles. These are the keys I look at before any other:

view = auto            # auto, split or unified (splits from 140 columns)
theme = tokyo-night    # 15 built-in themes
context = 3            # lines of context (-U)
syntax-diff = false    # off by default; I toggle it with 'd' in the viewer

dffy config --default lists every key with its value, and dffy themes shows the themes with a preview. Bindings are rewritten with keybind lines, including separate tables for the tree and the command panel:

keybind = ctrl+d=page_down
keybind = tree:x=mark_viewed

Where it falls short¶

  • It's a three-day-old project. The first public release is from 14 November, it's on 0.2.1 and it has 23 stars. That means config and flags can change without notice. I made it my pager anyway: if it breaks tomorrow, I'm back on delta in one command.
  • Git only. No Jujutsu, Mercurial or Sapling, which hunk and lumen do support. If you live in jj, this isn't for you.
  • No AI annotations. Lumen and hunk have an assistant layer on top of the diff; there's none of that here. The MCP server makes up for it, and that's the part I care about.
  • Renderer plugins are experimental: Markdown and Mermaid rendered inside the viewer, on r. It works, but it's clearly early.

The summary: delta decorates a diff, dffy reviews it. For a two-line patch I don't care which one I use, but for the 90% of diffs I actually read, I want the tree and the keys.

Original source: amalucelli/dffy

entry.title: degit: copy a repo without the history
entry.summary: degit copies the latest version of a Git repo without downloading the history and without leaving a .git behind. Hand it a GitHub /tree/main/... URL and it takes just that folder.
entry.content:
I needed the skills/find-skills folder from the vercel-labs/skills repo, a single 5.5 KB SKILL.md. Cloning the whole repo for that makes no sense at all, so I reached for degit, Rich Harris' tool (the Svelte guy) that does exactly this: pull a repo down without dragging the history along.

And it takes the browser URL as is, /tree/main/ and all.

What it does¶

It resolves the ref, downloads the tarball for that commit and unpacks it. No history, and no .git left underneath.

It works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Sourcehut and gists, and it's an npm package (Node 20 or later), so you can run it with npx without installing anything:

npx degit user/repo                  # latest version of the default branch
npx degit user/repo#v1.2.3           # tag, branch or commit
npx degit user/repo/subfolder        # just that folder
npx degit user/repo my-project       # into a new folder
npx degit user/repo my-project -F README.md,src   # just those files

The destination has to be empty unless you add --force. Tarballs are cached in ~/.cache/degit, and with --cache it won't even ask the network. The 3.x line, which is what you get today, adds -F/--files to keep loose files, aliases for the repos you come back to (degit alias github:user/repo myRepo) and an interactive mode when you run it with no arguments. For private repos it falls back to ssh, and that path does need git on your PATH.

Where it falls short¶

degit leaves you with a dead copy: no history, no remote, nothing to pull from. Perfect to start a project from a template, useless if you want to keep following the repo.

That's what git sparse-checkout is for, and it's still a real clone:

git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/user/repo
cd repo
git sparse-checkout set the/folder

Only that folder on disk, but with pull, branch switching and patches at hand. The difference between the two tools fits in one sentence: degit copies files, sparse-checkout brings you a repo with a narrower view.

Fuente original: Rich-Harris/degit

entry.title: Detecting secrets in git with gitleaks
entry.summary: gitleaks scans git repositories for secrets, API keys, and leaked credentials. Install it in seconds with gah — it might save you from a very bad day.
entry.content:
gitleaks scans git repositories —including the full commit history— for secrets: API keys, passwords, AWS tokens, database credentials, and over 150 predefined patterns.

Installing with gah¶

The fastest way on Linux is with gah, a GitHub release asset downloader:

$ gah install gitleaks/gitleaks
Fetching release info for: gitleaks/gitleaks [latest]
Found release: v8.30.1
Downloading: gitleaks_8.30.1_linux_x64.tar.gz
############################################### 100.0%
Verifying digest sha256 551f6fc8... ...
Digest verification succeeded!
Extracting: gitleaks_8.30.1_linux_x64.tar.gz
Installing: gitleaks
Done!

Single binary, zero dependencies, ready in seconds.

Basic usage¶

To scan a local repo with full commit history:

$ gitleaks git --verbose -v /path/to/repo

It walks every commit and shows what secrets it found, in which file and at which line.

Some useful flags:

  • --no-banner: hides the ASCII banner at startup.
  • --exit-code 0: don't exit with error when leaks are found (handy for CI).
  • --config .gitleaks.toml: use a custom config with your own detection rules.
  • --gitleaks-ignore-path .: respects the .gitleaksignore file for false positives.
  • --redact: masks secrets in output (useful for public logs).

You can also scan standalone directories with gitleaks dir or pipe content through gitleaks stdin.

When to use it¶

  • Before making a repo public: scan the full history to make sure no keys slipped through.
  • In CI/CD: add it as a GitHub Actions step so the build fails if someone commits a secret.
  • Security audits: great for reviewing old repos that have been touched by many people.

Pre-commit hook¶

The most effective way to use it is as a pre-commit hook that automatically blocks any commit containing secrets:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if [[ "${SKIP_GITLEAKS:-}" == "1" || "${SKIP_GITLEAKS:-}" == "true" ]]; then
  echo "Skipping gitleaks pre-commit scan because SKIP_GITLEAKS=${SKIP_GITLEAKS}." >&2
  exit 0
fi

if ! command -v gitleaks >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  cat >&2 <<'EOF'
gitleaks is required by this repository's pre-commit hook but was not found.
Install gitleaks, or set SKIP_GITLEAKS=1 for an intentional one-off bypass.
EOF
  exit 1
fi

echo "Running gitleaks on staged changes..." >&2
gitleaks protect --staged --source . --redact --no-banner

Save this as .githooks/pre-commit, make it executable (chmod +x), and configure git to use that directory:

git config core.hooksPath .githooks

From then on, every git commit will scan staged changes for secrets. Need to bypass it once? SKIP_GITLEAKS=1 git commit.

It's one of those tools you don't need until you really need it. And when that day comes, you'll be glad it's just a gah install away.

entry.title: Disable git autocrlf
entry.summary: If you use Windows (or WSL), Git has been silently converting your line endings. One command fixes it.
entry.content:
I'm not a regular Windows user, but if I were forced to use it for a while, WSL would be almost mandatory. Good to have this note handy (by Ryan Harrison).

If you're on Windows, Git has been silently messing with your line endings since the day you installed it. The culprit is core.autocrlf, enabled by default.

git config --global core.autocrlf false

What core.autocrlf does¶

Windows has historically used CRLF (\r\n) as its line ending character, while Linux and macOS use plain LF (\n). With autocrlf true (the default on Windows):

  • On checkout: Git converts LF line endings in the repository to CRLF in your working directory
  • On commit: Git converts CRLF back to LF before storing the file

In theory, your local files always have Windows-style line endings and the repository stays clean with Unix-style endings. In practice, it's a constant source of problems.

Why it's a bad default¶

WSL makes it worse. Your Linux environment expects LF line endings. Windows Git has helpfully checked out everything with CRLF. The result: every script and config file has a stray \r at the end of every line, causing silent failures. And if you haven't seen this warning, you've probably started ignoring it:

warning: LF will be replaced by CRLF in some-file.sh.
The file will have its original line endings in your working directory

Modern editors handle LF just fine. The original argument was that Notepad couldn't handle LF-only files — which was true in 2003. Notepad has supported LF line endings since Windows 10 (2018). VS Code, Sublime, Vim, IntelliJ, Notepad++ — they've all handled it fine for even longer.

The conversion is lossy in practice. Binary files can get corrupted if Git misidentifies them as text. If some people on a team have autocrlf true and others have it false, you'll end up with commits that are just line ending changes.

The fix: disable it and use .gitattributes¶

git config --global core.autocrlf false

From then on, Git leaves your line endings exactly as they are — no silent conversions. For teams, a .gitattributes file in the repository is a much better approach, since it applies the same rules for everyone regardless of their local config.

Use LF everywhere, configure your editor to save with LF by default. Don't think about it again (until you change machines).

Original source: Git - Disable autocrlf (Ryan Harrison)

entry.title: How I Use Git Worktrees for Concurrent Work
entry.summary: A practical approach to using git worktrees and maximizing productivity with multiple simultaneous work contexts
entry.content:
Aleksey Kladov shares his unique approach to using git worktrees, which goes beyond simply switching branches and becomes a complete methodology for concurrent work.

The Core Philosophy

"Git is not a version control system, Git is a toolbox for building a VCS"

This perspective completely changes how we think about git. Instead of limiting ourselves to basic functionalities, we can create our own optimized workflow.

The 5 Specialized Worktrees

The author maintains 5 worktrees, each with a specific purpose:

  1. main - Read-only snapshot - Clean reflection of remote main - Reference for comparisons - Never modified locally
  2. work - Main workspace - Day-to-day active development - Frequent commits with minimal messages - Detached HEAD for maximum flexibility
  3. review - Dedicated to code reviews - Clean context to analyze PRs - Without interfering with ongoing work
  4. fuzz - Long-running tests - Fuzzing and tests that last hours - Runs in parallel without blocking development
  5. scratch - Unrelated quick tasks - Experiments - Urgent fixes - Ad-hoc investigations
# Typical directory structure
~/projects/my-project/
├── main/        # main worktree
├── work/        # active development
├── review/      # reviews
├── fuzz/        # testing
└── scratch/     # experiments

Advantages of the Approach

Truly Concurrent Work
  • Multiple coding activities simultaneously
  • No need for stash or complex branch switching
  • Clean separation of contexts
Frictionless Workflow
  • Instant switching between tasks
  • Frequent commits without pressure for perfect messages
  • Free experimentation on detached HEAD
Real Parallelization
  • Fuzzing running while you develop
  • Reviews without interrupting main work
  • Background tests without blocks

Advanced Techniques

Strategic Detached HEAD

# In the 'work' worktree, work without a branch
git checkout --detach HEAD
# Frequent commit, reorganize later
git commit -m "wip"

Custom Scripts for Common Operations

# Script to quickly create/switch worktrees
#!/bin/bash
git worktree add "../$1" "$2"
cd "../$1"

Integration Flow

# From the 'work' worktree
git log --oneline  # review commits
git reset HEAD~5   # undo temporary commits
git add -p         # select changes
git commit         # clean final commit

Key Lessons

  1. Git is flexible: There is no "one right way" to use git
  2. Automate the repetitive: Custom scripts for common operations
  3. Separate contexts: Each type of work deserves its own space
  4. Cheap commits: Commit frequently, organize later

This approach transforms git from a versioning tool into a complete workflow management platform, maximizing productivity through truly concurrent work.

Original article: How I Use Git Worktrees
